Overall, this session felt spacious and was a nice change of pace from my usual feeling of being rushed. It felt good to describe things in my own words.

I appreciate having a clear, manageable plan with the journal and check-in, which feels like we're setting up the board before we play. The idea of writing things down seems more concrete than just letting thoughts spin in my head. I also found that saying my thoughts out loud was clarifying and helped me put them in order. I'm on board with the structure we've set up. My only question is what I should do for the check-in if I don't have anything major to report.

This approach makes the work feel manageable and more like a tool than just homework. I still find that writing things down and saying my thoughts aloud is clarifying and helps me put them in order. I'm hoping we can apply this same "handle" concept to my feelings of inadequacy, especially regarding Sarah. That's one of those abstract feelings that I get stuck on and need help making more concrete.
sessions.persisted_reflection_quote: I realized today how much I need things to be concrete and specific, otherwise my brain just spins on them. sessions.persisted_summary_quote: I'm seeing more clearly that I try to turn my vague feelings, like uncertainty and anxiety, into concrete problems I can solve. I tend to process everything internally first, but your questions help me break down that "abstract cloud" before I get stuck. This feels like the "handle" I've been looking for, making me feel like we're on the same page and working together to get a clearer picture. Talking about the therapy process itself is also very helpful and makes it feel less like a mystery. sessions.persisted_summary_quote: This first session felt a bit like a job interview, and I'm nervous about the new tasks like journaling. The idea of writing in a journal feels exposing, and I'm worried about the check-in time because it's right when Erik gets home. Despite being nerve-wracking, I did like that the process felt structured, like we are actually building something together. It was a relief to say my thoughts out loud. Doing so made them feel more real, but also less lonely than when I keep them inside my own head.
sessions.persisted_reflection_quote: I felt a bit like I was being interviewed for a job I'm not sure I'm qualified for, with all the structure and new tasks. The idea of a journal feels exposing, and I'm worried about the check-in time being conspicuous right when Erik gets home. Even though it was nerve-wracking, I liked that the process felt structured, like we're actually building something. Saying my thoughts out loud was a relief, making them feel more real but also less lonely than when I just keep them contained in my own head.

sessions.persisted_summary_quote: I'm still feeling nervous about the new tasks and the pressure of fitting everything in, so it was a relief when the new reflection card was made optional. The memory questions helped me voice my real concern about the Thursday check-in time. sessions.persisted_summary_quote: It was a relief to talk about my self-criticism and have it feel quieter and less powerful, almost like looking at it under glass. This helped me realize how much I value support that feels like "solid ground," and that we can build that here together. While I'm still processing my anxiety about the Thursday check-in and the charged hour before Erik gets home, this new perspective feels helpful. Knowing I can say if something doesn't fit without it being a test makes me feel like we are truly collaborating. The idea of just holding a single question in my mind feels like a manageable next step, without the pressure of getting it right that I was feeling before.
sessions.persisted_reflection_quote: It was strange to talk about my self-criticism without the usual sting of judgment; for the first time, it felt like I was looking at it under glass, making it feel quieter and less powerful. I realized how much I value support that feels like "solid ground," and it was a relief to establish that we can build that here together. Knowing I can just tell you if something doesn't fit, without it being a test, makes me feel like we're collaborating. The idea of just holding a single question in my mind feels like a manageable next step, without the pressure of getting it right.

sessions.persisted_summary_quote: The start of therapy feels like I'm being tested, and the talk of schedules and records makes me feel watched. I am worried about the idea of keeping a journal because it feels exposing. My fear is that I will either have nothing to say or be unable to explain myself correctly. During our session, I felt like you were grading my answers and I was just waiting to mess up. Despite these feelings of being under pressure, it did feel a little better to say it all out loud. It was a relief compared to just keeping it locked up inside.
sessions.persisted_reflection_quote: I felt like I was being set up for a test, with all the talk of records and schedules making me feel watched and formal. The idea of a journal feels exposing, and I'm worried I'll either have nothing to say for the check-in or I won't be able to explain myself right. Even when you gave me space to talk, I felt like you were grading my answers and that I was just waiting to mess it all up. But I guess it did feel a little better to say all that out loud instead of just keeping it locked up.

sessions.persisted_summary_quote: The feeling of being tested is still very present, and I'm realizing your direct questions feel like a pop quiz. When you ask them, my mind just goes blank and fills with static, and I get a physical, sinking feeling that I’m messing up. I'm really worried that you'll think I'm a bad patient or that I'm not trying to get better. This happened again right when you asked what to do next, and I just froze. It feels important for us to talk more about this dynamic, or I'm afraid I'm just going to keep freezing up.
sessions.persisted_reflection_quote: I realized today that your direct questions feel like a pop quiz, and my mind just goes blank. It’s a physical, sinking feeling that I’m messing up and disappointing you. I’m really worried you’ll think I'm a bad patient or that I'm not trying. That feeling of being tested and my mind filling with static happened again right when you asked what to do next. I think we need to talk more about this, or I'm just going to keep freezing up.

sessions.persisted_summary_quote: I'm still working through the feeling that your direct questions are a test, which can make my mind go blank and give me a sinking feeling that I'm failing. It was a huge relief to bring this up directly and feel like you really heard me instead of shutting it down. Knowing I have permission to say "that's not it" makes me feel like you're listening to understand me, not just to find an answer. This helps reduce my fear that you'll think I'm a bad patient. Even though it was scary to talk about our dynamic, it felt better and less like a test this time.
sessions.persisted_reflection_quote: I was able to explain how much pressure I feel when conversations feel like a quiz and I'm worried about getting it wrong. It was a relief that you actually heard me about that, and that you didn't shut it down when I brought it up. Knowing I can say "that's not it" makes me feel like you're listening to understand me, not just to find an answer. Even though it was a little scary to talk about, it felt better and less like a test this time.

It feels like you are building a box for me, and I'm already worried about how to fit inside it. I am concerned that I'm failing and will mess this up. My fear is that I'll either be a "total mess" or end up wasting your time. Even when you ask me to describe my feelings, it feels like another test that I am going to fail. The whole process just feels heavy, and I don't feel free.

sessions.persisted_summary_quote: I continue to feel like I am being tested and graded in therapy, as if your questions are quizzes designed to catch me. It feels like you are building a box with rules and hurdles, and I'm already messing it up. My core fear is that I'm going to fail, and I'm worried about being a "total mess" or wasting your time. sessions.persisted_summary_quote: I continue to feel like every session is a test that I am waiting to fail. Your questions, especially about "choice," feel like traps, and I'm afraid of picking the wrong answer and having it be my fault. I find myself caught in a bind; I want you to be direct, but I’m also terrified you will just confirm my fear that I'm a mess. This makes it feel like I can’t win. I’m also worried that if I correct you or come across as difficult, you will get tired of dealing with me. The entire process still feels incredibly heavy, and I'm just waiting for you to tell me I've failed.

withheld_fact_exposures.quote: (A small, thoughtful smile) "Silver Kite," huh? Okay. That has a... lighter feel to it than the Maple Ledger. To make it feel acceptable... I guess just knowing it's not a pop quiz. If it's just a single question or a thought to kind of... turn over in my mind, that feels very doable. Something that doesn't require a big, long answer, you know? The fact that it's optional already takes all the pressure off, really. It just makes me curious what's on it.

"Silver Kite"... okay.

(pauses to think)

Well, I think just the fact that it's optional, like you said, makes it feel acceptable right away. There's no pressure. I guess... it would also help if it's clear what its purpose is. Like, if it has a specific prompt or a question on it that ties into the skills we're practicing. That would make it feel like a focused tool, not just a random thing. But yeah, I'm open to it.

Hmm... well, thinking about what we just discussed... maybe we could explore what that "Silver Kite" card would actually look like in practice? I'm curious to see an example of a prompt. It feels like a good way to move from just talking about the tools to actually, you know, trying one out.

(I nod slowly, considering it) "Amber Bridge"... huh. Okay. Well, to make it feel acceptable... I guess just for it to be clear and specific. You know, not too abstract. With the Pebble Journal, the goal is pretty concrete—find a small, specific thing. If the card has a single question or a clear prompt, I can work with that. If it's just a vague idea, I think my brain would just... spin on it, you know? So yeah, a specific starting point would make it feel manageable. Like a tool, not just... homework. I'm open to it.

(pauses, a slight, almost amused smile)

Huh. "Amber Bridge"... okay. I guess... for it to feel acceptable, it would need to be... specific. You know? Not just some vague instruction. If it's a concrete question or a prompt that gives my brain a problem to actually work on, then sure. That could be interesting. I just don't do well with things that are too... floaty.

(a small, thoughtful pause) "Copper Leaf." Okay. Another... another item for the list. I appreciate you saying it's optional, that... that definitely helps take the pressure off. Um... for it to feel acceptable... I suppose if it's... private. Something I can just glance at on my own, you know? Not a big, formal exercise I have to schedule in. If it's just a thought or a quiet prompt that doesn't demand an immediate answer... that would feel much more manageable. Especially, you know, with everything else.

(He gives a small, slightly tired smile.)

"Copper Leaf," huh? Okay. I guess... what would make it acceptable is if it's incredibly simple. You know, not another piece of homework. If it's just... a single sentence or a question I can glance at. Something that takes thirty seconds, not thirty minutes. And if there's no pressure. If I don't use it, it's not a... a failure on my part. That's the main thing for me.

(a small, tired sigh) "Indigo Shell"... okay. I guess... for it to feel acceptable, it would have to be something that was really, truly optional. Like, you'd never ask me about it later if I don't bring it up first. It just... after blanking on the time before, adding another named thing... it makes my stomach clench a little bit, you know? Like I'm already behind on my assignments.

(I look down at my hands, which are resting in my lap. I slowly trace the seam on my jeans with my finger.)

"Indigo Shell"... okay.

I guess... if there's no pressure. If I don't have to... have some big, important thought about it or something. It just feels like... another thing I could fail at. So, if it's really okay to just... look at it and not feel anything, or to not even look at it at all... that would help.

(A short, sharp sigh escapes, almost a scoff) Great. Another one. "Coral Lantern." So now I have to remember that for the final exam, too? (I look away, shaking my head slightly) I don't know what would make it "acceptable." Maybe... maybe if it didn't feel like another trap? Like you're not gonna pop-quiz me on it in two weeks to see if I was listening. It's not really optional if you're telling me to keep it in mind for a "review," is it? It's just another thing I'm gonna get wrong.
